methodological_rigor.justification: Large registry-based retrospective cohort (N=116,217 co-test samples) with clear inclusion/exclusion criteria, deterministic linkage via national personal identification number, standardized cytology (Bethesda 2014), and a well-defined HPV mRNA assay (PreTect SEE). Outcomes are histologically adjudicated with p16 IHC adjunct and worst-diagnosis rule, with passive follow-up through December 2025. Limitations acknowledged include verification bias (test-positives more likely to undergo biopsy), sample-level rather than woman-level unit of analysis, absence of HPV DNA co-testing across the full cohort, and no formal health-economic evaluation. Statistics are appropriate: absolute risks with 95% CIs, risk ratios with CIs, risk differences, Pearson chi-square for overall comparisons, mutually exclusive genotype-combination analysis to address marker overlap, and cautious interpretation of sparse cervical-cancer cells.

clinical_relevance_loe.justification: Large individual cohort study of a diagnostic co-testing strategy in routine clinical practice corresponds to Oxford LoE 2b. Clinical relevance is direct—results inform triage thresholds and follow-up intensity for women with NILM cytology (identifying a 1.3% subgroup with ~26-fold higher cancer risk) and ASC-US+ cytology (concentrating 77.6% of cancers in mRNA-positive), which is actionable for screening-program design, particularly in mixed transition or low-resource settings.

reporting_quality.justification: As a diagnostic accuracy/risk-stratification study, STARD is most applicable (though elements of STROBE also apply). Reporting is thorough: setting, eligibility, index test, reference standard, flow of samples (123,674 initially, 116,217 analyzed), absolute risks with 95% CIs, effect sizes, and limitations. A formal STARD flow diagram and checklist are not explicitly shown, and verification bias is discussed but not quantitatively corrected. Data availability score is 2 because de-identified registry data from a hospital laboratory information system are unlikely to be openly shared without restricted access; no public repository or analysis code is mentioned, and ethical approvals reference only local access.

novelty_literature.justification: PreTect SEE and HPV E6/E7 mRNA triage are established concepts (refs 17, 20, 21, 23, 24, 25, 29) and prior Norwegian cohorts exist (ref 24 is a Northern Norway cohort with 8-10 year follow-up from the same group/region). This work's incremental contributions are the large sample size (~116k co-tests), the mutually exclusive genotype-combination analysis, and the real-world mix of screening/follow-up/clinically indicated testing. It is a meaningful extension rather than a paradigm shift.

writing_presentation.justification: The manuscript is well-organized with clear separation between four co-test categories, sub-analyses within NILM and ASC-US+, and genotype-specific results. Numerical reporting is precise and consistent (95% CIs throughout, RRs, risk differences). Discussion is thoughtful and appropriately calibrated (explicitly noting that findings do not challenge HPV DNA primary screening). Some sections are repetitive between Results and Discussion, and tables/figures are referenced but not included in the normalized text.

key_strengths: Very large real-world cohort (n=116,217 co-test samples) with deterministic linkage via national personal ID and long passive follow-up through December 2025

Clear stepwise risk gradient across four co-test categories with 95% CIs, RRs, and risk differences; NILM/mRNA+ identifies a 1.3% subgroup concentrating 42.7% of within-NILM CIN3+ and 25% of within-NILM cancers
Genotype-specific analyses (HPV16 > HPV18 > HPV45) with both marker-specific and mutually exclusive combination approaches to address co-expression
Thoughtful, calibrated discussion that positions findings as complementary to HPV DNA primary screening rather than as a replacement
Transparent limitations including verification bias, sample-level unit of analysis, and lack of HPV DNA co-testing in the full cohort
key_concerns: Verification bias from passive follow-up where test-positives are more likely to undergo biopsy than double-negatives (acknowledged but not quantitatively corrected)
Unit of analysis is the co-test sample, not the woman—repeated testing may inflate event counts
Novelty is incremental—PreTect SEE has been evaluated in overlapping Northern Norway cohorts by the same authors (ref 24)
No formal STARD checklist/flow diagram despite the diagnostic-accuracy nature of the work
No open data or analytic code; data availability is limited to the laboratory information system
No cost-effectiveness or formal program-level analysis
chief_reviewer.rationale: Well-executed large registry-based diagnostic/risk-stratification cohort with clear clinical interpretability and honest limitations; solid mid-tier publication with minor revisions to add a STARD checklist, sensitivity analyses for verification bias, and a woman-level sensitivity analysis.
